messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About the Riemannian geometry in Stan
parts:
Hi Stephen,

We currently don't have a targeted version for a release version of Riemannian HMC. An implementation of the algorithm has been available in the source code for quite some time (thanks to Michael!).

There are at least two technical challenges before we would be comfortable releasing it (and we'd love help):
1. implementing higher order automatic differentiation for functions in the Stan language
  - currently, we're able to differentiate (get gradients) through all of the functions in the Stan language (there are ways to intentionally break this, but we try to not make it easy)
  - we don't have the same for higher order automatic differentiation, which is required for RHMC
2. compiling
  - it won't work on Windows under the gcc 4.6.3 compiler. I'm not sure if it's a problem with the new RTools compiler

For tradeoffs, see Andrew's email. There's the additional time of compilation time. We haven't experimented too much, but higher order autodiff takes much longer to compile.


Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About the Riemannian geometry in Stan
parts:
As to (1), I think they're implemented pretty much everywhere
other than for the ODE solver, but they're not tested thoroughly,
which amounts to the same thing for us.

And yes, Riemannian involves an O(N^3) matrix decomposition for
dimension N problems at each step, whereas Euclidean NUTS with
diagonal mass matrix is only O(N) per step. In cases of high
curvature, the Euclidean algorithm will fail or grind to a halt
with a very high constant factor due to small step size.

- Bob

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About the Riemannian geometry in Stan
parts: So it really depends on the problem at hand. With high curvature, euclidean will often fail or will explore slowly due to smaller step sizes needed. Otoh, with high curvature, riemannian will not fail or explore slowly, but per-step it will take longer. So if you have regions of the posterior with large curvature, Riemannian could mix and explore faster (or more sample more efficiently) than euclidean, whereas with less difficult curvature euclidean may be more efficient?
